Playing guitar.

I spent 12 years teaching myself to play, playing in bands and ultimately putting out a vinyl record to 'wrap it up'. Along with a number of other factors out of my control, I lost the drive and love to play. I want to pick it back up, but keep finding reasons not to...and my now ex got me a bad ass tele last year that I've barely touched.

Right, well, I'll drop the tip I usually have for people who ask me to teach them to play. I've had a guitar around and played it daily now for 20ish years. This is the best, simplest advice for learning and getting motivated to play.

Get a guitar stand, if you don't have one, set up the guitar somewhere you will pass by often or spend a lot of time near. Whenever you get the chance, pick it up. The rest will happen naturally. Picking up the guitar has to become the most easy, natural and unemcumbered act.

I keep a baby acoustic next to the computer at home and I'm constantly reaching for it to the point where I play guitar most often in my computer chair. Website loading slow? Computer needs a reboot? Turn the chair, lean over and pick it up. Quite often I find myself browsing the web with the thing in my lap.

From there, you learn or remember to play again, to pick it up without purpose and do what you want. If you don't know what to do, try something. As a kid, my first experiences playing with a guitar were making funny words into the soundhole. But don't make too much of it. Don't think of what to play, or that you even have to. All you have to do is pick it up when you have a moment, because it's been left so temptingly at hand.

Cheers, thanks. I do have them all over the house; well, the house is small enough they're pretty close at hand, I have an acoustic lying on my bed at the moment.

Fasting.

If you can make it past the fourth day, you'll be in a euphoric state that is tough to describe. You feel invincible yet weak/tired at the same time, you sleep less, your body temperature goes down a degree or two (I felt cold all the time), your brain goes into overdrive, and everything is experienced in a slightly different, weird, dream-like or trance-like way. But those first and fourth days are fairly brutal. Strangely, two and three are never so bad for me. I think it may have something to do with the 72-hour starvation-mode cutoff.

When I fasted 22 days I measured my ketones on an abbott meter and they got up to the five to seven range (usually five or six) a few times. Most people would exhibit zero, maybe 0.1 first thing in the morning. Diabetic ketoacidosis happens around eleven. So I was getting up there but not to a dangerous level. My blood glucose was pretty low compared to normal.

I took 2-3 mile jogs in the evenings, and I was completely at ease as long as I went slow. It's crazy to think what the individual cells are capable of surviving when they are in "we gotta get through this famine" mode. It also made me realize in a deeper way that we didn't get to the top of the food chain by being weaklings who couldn't survive a while without food.

I don't necessarily avoid it, but practically speaking it's only possible every so often. I also tend to be really careful about it, planning and preparing ahead of time for things like electrolytes and stuff going on at work (stress levels). I've had several aborts where something just didn't go right and I couldn't go through with it.

I think it's something a lot more westerners should at least look into (just for the weight-loss alone).
